Overview
Various etiologies for knee pain exist, including
Traumatic
Congenital
Infectious
Ischemic/osteonecrosis
Referred
Inflammatory
Osteoarthritic

Overview
Persistent knee pain affects approximately 25% of adults.1 Although a number of
etiologies exist for persistent, or chronic, knee pain, the most common etiology of knee
pain is osteoarthritis, with symptomatic osteoarthritis affecting more than 15% of
Americans older than 50 years.2
Surgeons must differentiate the various etiologies of knee pain, which can be
accomplished via a thorough patient history and a comprehensive physical examination.
Neuroanatomy of Knee Pain
The posterior knee is innervated by the superomedial and inferomedial genicular nerves,
which are branches of the tibial distribution of the sciatic nerve. There are also contributions
of the obturator nerve to innervation of the medial and posterior knee.
The anterior knee receives innervation from the suprapatellar and infrapatellar genicular
nerves, which are branches of the saphenous nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve. In
addition, the anterior knee is innervated by the superolateral genicular nerve, a branch of the
common peroneal nerve distribution of the sciatic nerve.3
Hip disease may manifest as knee pain referred along common neural pathways. In general,
the obturator nerve is the commonality.
As a result, in evaluating a patient with knee pain, it is important to evaluate the ipsilateral
hip as a possible cause.

Neuroanatomy of Knee Pain
The innervation of the knee is responsible for pain that patients experience. Knowledge
of the nerves that cause pain in each region of the knee enables surgeons to more
precisely target pain blockades (eg, via radiofrequency ablation of genicular nerves). In
addition, knowledge of the innervation of the knee may help surgeons determine if pain
is referred or originating from the knee. Innervation to the knee joint is from the
genicular nerves, which arise from branches of the sciatic, femoral, and obturator
nerves.3
Arthridities of the Knee

Arthridities of the Knee
Arthridities of the knee are common causes of knee pain. Osteoarthritis followed by
rheumatoid arthritis and seronegative inflammatory arthritis are the most common
arthridities of the knee. These etiologies of knee pain result in loss of articular cartilage
as the disease process progresses. Surgeons must understand the responsible disease
process in each patient because it may affect perioperative complication risks,4 such as
the risk of infection and the risk of revision (Figure 1), and may affect important surgical
considerations, such as the level of constraint necessary if surgical management is
indicated.

Osteoarthritis
Characterized by mechanical wear and tear of articular cartilage in the knee joint.
Water content and permeability of articular cartilage increases during the osteoarthritic
process; degradation of proteoglycans also increases.
Features of osteoarthritis include loss of articular cartilage, osteophyte formation, and
remodeling of subchondral bone resulting in subchondral sclerosis and cysts5 (Figure 2).
Prevalence increases with age; osteoarthritis is the most common cause of chronic knee pain
and disability in patients older than 50 years.
Etiology for knee osteoarthritis is multifactorial.
Risk factors for knee osteoarthritis include6
Obesity

Previous knee trauma
Hand osteoarthritis
Increasing age
Sex (women at increased risk)
Genetics
Medial compartment knee osteoarthritis is most common. This is because approximately 65%
of the forces go through the medial side of a normal knee joint.
Healthcare expenditures in the management of knee osteoarthritis exceed $27 billion
annually.
Figure 2 AP knee radiographs demonstrate the Kellgren-Lawrence classification of osteoarthritis.
A, Grade 1 osteoarthritis, which includes doubtful narrowing of the joint space with possible

osteophyte formation. B, Grade 2 osteoarthritis, which includes possible narrowing of the joint
space with definite osteophyte formation. C, Grade 3 osteoarthritis, which includes definite
narrowing of joint space, moderate osteophyte formation, some sclerosis, and possible deformity
of bony ends. D, Grade 4 osteoarthritis, which includes large osteophyte formation, severe
narrowing of the joint space with marked sclerosis, and definite deformity of bony ends.
(Reproduced with permission from Kellgren JH, Lawrence JS: Radiological assessment of osteo-
arthrosis. Ann Rheum Dis 1957;16[4]:494-502.)
Rheumatoid Arthritis
Systemic, autoimmune disease process involving synovium
Affects less than 1% of the US population
Approximately 3% to 4% of patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty (TKA) have rheumatoid
arthritis.7
Disease process involves receptor activator of nuclear factor-κ B ligand secretion by synovial
fibroblasts, resulting in periarticular joint erosions.
Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs have substantially altered the natural history of the
disease, slowing progression of many sequalae and decreasing morbidity.
It is important to understand which disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs or corticosteroid
medications a patient is taking because some of these medications should be withheld
perioperatively to minimize wound complications or infection risk8 (Table 1).
Radiographs may demonstrate osteopenia, periarticular erosions, lack of osteophytes, or
symmetrical loss of joint space throughout the knee9 (Figure 3).
Risk factors for rheumatoid arthritis include
Genetics
HLA-DR4 is linked to rheumatoid arthritis
Sex (women at increased risk)
Northern European descent
Because it is a disease process of the synovium, all compartments of the knee are affected.
Preoperatively, it is important to obtain cervical spine radiographs (flexion/extension) to
evaluate for atlantoaxial or subaxial instability.
Postoperatively, patients with rheumatoid arthritis have an increased risk for fracture and
prosthetic joint infection.

Seronegative Inflammatory Arthridities
Autoimmune processes, which may include psoriatic arthritis, lupus, reactive arthritis, and
ankylosing spondylitis
Psoriatic arthritis affects as much as 0.25% of the population. Patients may have a combination
of erosive and proliferative radiographic findings, including fluffy periostitis and erosive
periarticular joint changes.10
May present with systemic manifestations and polyarticular arthritis
Require preoperative medical workup to evaluate for and optimize cardiac and pulmonary
manifestations of disease

As with rheumatoid arthritis medications, it is important to understand which medications a
patient is taking because many may need to be withheld perioperatively to minimize wound
complications or infection risk.
Psoriatic plaques have increased levels of bacteria. Standard skin sterilization processes have
not fully decreased bacterial burden in these plaques; therefore, these skin lesions should be
treated preoperatively by a dermatologist, and incisions through psoriatic plaques should be
avoided. In addition, postoperative psoriatic plaques may develop around the skin incision in
patients with psoriatic arthritis;10 this is known as the Koebner phenomenon10 (Figure 4).
Ankylosing spondylitis predisposes patients to an increased risk of postoperative stiffness and
heterotopic ossification formation11 (Figure 5). Heterotopic ossification prophylaxis via
radiation or medication may be considered in this patient population.

Knee Physical Examination
Inspection
With the patient standing, evaluate the affected and unaffected knees.
Inspect the knees for lesions, erythema/discoloration, and previous incisions.
Assess alignment (ie, varus, valgus, neutral) visually (Figure 6); compare with the
contralateral side. This is important because intraoperative considerations and the risk of
potential complications are different in patients with a varus knee and patients with a valgus
knee (Video 1).
Assess patellar height (baja, alta, or neutral).

Assess for quadriceps atrophy (patients with knee pain often favor the other limb, leading to
atrophy about the thigh of the affected limb).
Figure 6 Clinical photograph of a patient with a knee flexion contracture, which often is
associated with a concurrent hip flexion contracture, and valgus alignment. A crouched posture
results in high-energy demands because the hip, knee, and ankle extensors must be active
continuously to maintain an upright posture. This limits the time and distance a person is able to
walk. (Reproduced from Baldwin K, Keenan MA: Normal and pathologic gait, in Lieberman JR, ed:
AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2014, pp 179-187.)

arthroplasty: Video vignettes. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of

Gait
Evaluate the gait pattern while the patient remains upright.
Assess for antalgic (defined as limited time in stance phase) or painful gait.
Identify potential varus or valgus thrust (coronal plane dynamic instabilities concerning for
ligamentous damage).12
Varus thrust is a dynamic increase in varus alignment during the stance phase of gait.
Valgus thrust is less common than varus thrust.
Range of motion
Normal flexion: 0° to 160°
Preoperative range of motion is most predictive of range of motion after TKA.13
Palpation
Evaluate for effusion by milking fluid from the suprapatellar pouch and examining for
ballottability of the patella.
Palpate for cysts about the knee, such as a posterior popliteal cyst (Baker cyst).
Assess the medial, lateral, and patellofemoral compartments for pain.
Palpate the medial and lateral joint lines to evaluate for arthritic pain.
Pain in the medial or lateral joint lines indicates disease in that compartment.

Can also palpate the medial condyle, lateral femoral condyle, and pes anserine insertion to
differentiate pain from arthritis versus ligament injury or tendonitis
To evaluate patellofemoral joint pain on examination, perform a patellar grind test, in
which an axial force and a medial/lateral force are applied to the patella to grind it against
the trochlea. The patient is instructed to contract the quadriceps. Pain in response to this
examination is a positive finding for patellofemoral compartment pain.
Ligamentous evaluation/provocative tests
Medial collateral ligament (MCL)
Apply a valgus force to the knee at 0° and 30° of flexion.
At 0°, evaluating a combination of MCL, capsular, and anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)
contributions to stability. At 30° of flexion, isolating the MCL contribution to coronal plane
stability. Gapping of less than 5 mm is normal.
In the coronal plane, bone loss or substantial medial compartment arthritis may result in
pseudosubluxation, which may mimic MCL looseness. Alignment of the joint should be
considered during this examination maneuver to differentiate ligamentous etiology from
progressive arthritic process.
Lateral collateral ligament (LCL)
Apply a varus force to the knee at 0° and 30° of flexion
At 0°, evaluating a combination of LCL, capsular, and ACL contributions to stability. At 30°
of flexion, isolating the LCL contribution to coronal plane stability. Gapping of less than 5
mm is normal.
Posterior cruciate ligament
Posterior drawer test: With the knee flexed at 90°, apply a posterior force on the tibia to
evaluate for posterior translation. The anterior aspect of the tibia should be at the level of
the condyles if the test is initiated. Translation of less than 5 mm is normal.
Knowledge of posterior cruciate ligament competency is important in considering cruciate-
retaining TKA.
ACL
Anterior drawer test: With the knee flexed at 90°, apply an anterior force on the tibia to
evaluate for anterior translation. Translation of less than 5 mm is normal.
Lachman test (Figure 7): With the knee flexed to 30°, stabilize the distal femur with one
hand and apply an anterior force on the tibia with other hand. Translation of less than 5
mm is normal.
The Lachman test is more sensitive for ACL deficiency compared with the anterior drawer
test.

Hip and spine must be evaluated to ensure they are not contributing to knee pain.

Knee Physical Examination
Physical examination of the knee is critically important and vital to determine the correct
diagnosis. Physical examination begins with observation of the knee and its mechanics,
which is accomplished via inspection, observation of gait, and evaluation of range of
motion. The next portions of the physical examination, including palpation and
provocative tests, may generate pain. The purpose of the potential pain-generating
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | History and Physical Examination of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000016
17/33

portion of the physical examination is to identify structural pathology in the knee that
may be generating pain (ie, meniscal tear, cartilage wear in a specific compartment).
Every physical examination for knee pain should include an evaluation of the hip and the
spine because pathology in these anatomic structures may refer pain to the knee.
Important History and Physical Examination Findings to
Differentiate Diagnoses About the Knee
Pain
Location
Anterior knee pain: Consistent with patellofemoral joint pain. Patients with patellofemoral
pain also may have difficulty negotiating stairs or with prolonged sitting because of stresses
on the patellofemoral joint.
Medial knee pain: Consistent with medial compartment disease, such as arthritis, but also
may be present with meniscal injury or MCL injury. Physical examination is useful to
differentiate ligamentous pain from arthritic/meniscal pain.
Lateral knee pain: Concerning for lateral compartment disease, such as arthritis. Physical
examination is useful to differentiate LCL pain from arthritic/meniscal pain.
Posterior knee pain: Common with knee arthritis because swelling can stretch the posterior
capsule, causing pain with knee extension.
Epicondyles/pes anserine: may represent ligamentous/bursitic etiologies of pain
Character
Soreness, achy, sharp, dull: all may be consistent with arthritis pain
Radiating/burning: This type of pain, especially with radiation into the foot, is more
concerning for neurogenic pain that may not have an intra-articular knee etiology.
Knee corticosteroid/lidocaine injection can be used for diagnostic purposes if this type of
pain is present to determine intra-articular knee contribution.
Chronology
Pain at the beginning of the day that improves with ambulation is more consistent with
pain from inflammatory arthritis.
Pain with weight bearing and increased activity that is the worst at the end of day is more
consistent with osteoarthritis or osteonecrosis.

loosening.
Pain present with and without activity and during the night is concerning for infection.
Difficulty negotiating stairs or uneven ground
This may be present with osteoarthritis.
In patients who have undergone previous TKA, it may be present in situations of an
unresurfaced patella or instability.
Hip pathology
Patient also may have groin pain
Evaluate via imaging studies (AP pelvis radiograph)
Examination suggestive of hip pathology includes
Limited or painful hip range of motion
Log roll test

Important History and Physical Examination Findings to
Differentiate Diagnoses About the Knee
In examining patients with knee pain, the surgeon should ask about the location,
character, and chronology of the pain. It also is important to understand how uneven
ground and stairs affect the patient. Then, a physical examination is performed to better
understand the status of the patient’s knees.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | History and Physical Examination of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000016
20/33

Surgeons must note pertinent findings during the patient history and deviations from
normal during the physical examination. These findings will aid in making the correct
diagnosis. During the patient history, surgeons must identify the location of pain. For
example, anterior knee pain often is associated with patellofemoral joint pathology. In
addition, surgeons must understand the character of the pain. Pain that is described as
sore or dull often is arthritic, whereas pain described as burning or electrical often is
radicular pain from the spine. Next, surgeons must determine the timeline, or
chronology, of the symptoms. Acute pain and chronic pain tend to have different
etiologies. Similarly, pain that worsens with activity rather than pain that improves with
activity may help differentiate osteoarthritic pathology from inflammatory pathology.
Lastly, surgeons must consider other etiologies for knee pain (ie, the spine or hip).
Surgeons must consider these etiologies in patients who do not have reproducible pain
during a knee examination and/or have knee imaging studies that appear benign.
Effect of Previous Surgery and Modifiable and Nonmodifiable
Comorbidities

Effect of Previous Surgery and Modifiable and Nonmodifiable
Comorbidities
In obtaining a patient’s history, surgeons must understand the injury and the surgical
history of the affected joint. Prior injury may predispose patients to posttraumatic
arthritis, which may influence postoperative TKA outcomes and complications. In
addition, prior hardware may interfere with planned TKA; therefore, templating and
planning for possible removal are essential. In patients who have undergone prior
surgery, surgeons must consider the placement of prior incisions to plan the incision for
the current surgical procedure. In addition to prior surgical procedures and prior
trauma, patient comorbidities have a considerable effect on perioperative complications;
therefore, this information must be obtained via a thorough patient history so
preoperative optimization may be performed.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:23 PM
AAOS | History and Physical Examination of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000016

Influence of Previous Surgery
Fracture: It is important to understand fractures sustained about the knee because they may
predispose patients to posttraumatic arthritis and affect TKA outcome.
Tibial plateau fracture
Posttraumatic knee osteoarthritis occurs in 25% to 45% of patients who have a tibial
plateau fracture. Patients who undergo conversion from open reduction and internal
fixation of a tibial plateau fracture to TKA have a higher rate of complications compared
with those who did not have a previous fracture.15 This should be discussed preoperatively
with the patient.
Patellar fracture
Patellar fracture before TKA does not influence implant survivorship but negatively affects
postoperative TKA range of motion.16 A previous patellar fracture may influence whether to
perform a patellar resurfacing.
Femoral or tibial fracture
In patients with a prior femoral or tibial fracture (Figure 10), surgeons must determine if
intramedullary hardware may affect the surgical technique for TKA, requiring computer
navigation or extramedullary alignment guides.
In addition, if malalignment that occurred during healing of the fracture may need to be
corrected in staged fashion before TKA.

Figure 10 Radiographs of a knee with a valgus deformity and a retained tibial nail. Preoperative
AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs demonstrate a severe valgus deformity with a retained
Kuntscher nail in the tibia. Postoperative AP (C) and lateral (D) radiographs demonstrate
correction of the deformity with the use of a pie-crusting technique via a medial paraptellar
approach. The Kuntscher nail was retained by using a short-pegged tantalum-coated tibial
component with cemented fixation because of poor bone quality.(Reproduced from Baldini A,
Castellani L, Traverso F, Balatri A, Balato G, Franceschini V: The difficult primary total knee
arthroplasty: A review. Bone Joint J 2015;97[10 suppl A]:30-39.)
Soft-tissue or osteotomy procedures: Knowledge of other procedures a patient may have
undergone about the knee is important because it may influence surgical technique, surgical
treatment options, and safety of the surgical approach.
Previous knee arthroscopy
Knowledge of the compartment the patient may have had soft-tissue procedures in is
important because it may affect whether unicompartmental procedures are appropriate.
In addition, patients who have undergone arthroscopy before TKA may have an increased
risk for revision TKA. This should be discussed preoperatively with the patient.17
Previous ACL reconstruction
Injury to the ACL influences wear and osteoarthritis patterns in the knee. ACL-competent
knees are associated with anteromedial wear patterns, whereas ACL-incompetent knees
are associated with posteromedial wear patterns.

Previous ACL reconstruction makes primary TKA more difficult, with longer surgical times
and increased risk of revision.18 This should be discussed preoperatively with the patient.
Previous tibial tubercle osteotomies for patellar instability
Hauser procedure (Figure 11); posteromedialization of the tibial tubercle performed for
recurrent patellar instability
This needs to be known preoperatively because this procedure places the patellar tendon
at risk during medial parapatellar arthrotomy. Patellar tendon disruption has occurred
during primary TKA in patients who have undergone a previous Hauser procedure.19
Maquet procedure: anteriorization of the tibial tubercle to off load the patellofemoral joint,
performed to minimize patellofemoral arthrosis
This distortion of the tibial tubercle needs to be known preoperatively because surgeons
reference this landmark for rotational orientation of the tibial component. This procedure
also may influence access to the intramedullary canal, if necessary.20

High tibial osteotomy: This osteotomy is used to correct varus alignment in patients with early
osteoarthritis. Knowledge of previous procedures is important because surgical scarring may
influence TKA incision placement, and hardware often may interfere with TKA surgical
technique (Video 2).
In addition, conversion from high tibial osteotomy to TKA may be associated with similar
patient-reported outcomes compared with primary TKA but with substantially higher revision
rates.21 This should be discussed preoperatively with the patient.
Previous arthroplasty procedures: Knowledge of whether a patient has undergone previous
unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, TKA, or revision TKA is important because it influences
potential etiologies for pain and required workup.

Influence of Comorbidities
Outcomes and complications of arthroplasty are related to surgical technique and
optimization of comorbidities. Therefore, in obtaining a patient’s history, surgeons must
understand the patient’s comorbidity burden. Comorbidities that influence perioperative
complications include obesity, diabetes mellitus, hepatitis C, smoking, and others (Video 3).
Obesity
Obesity is a growing problem, with nearly 40% of the US population being classified as
obese based on body mass index.
Patients with obesity who undergo arthroplasty have an increased risk for perioperative
infection and poorer implant survivorship.23

For patients with morbid obesity (body mass index >40 kg/m2), weight loss of 20 lb
preoperatively is associated with advantages with regard to postoperative hospital length
of stay and increased likelihood of discharge to home.24
Patients with obesity should be counseled on the importance of weight loss before TKA.
Nutritional consultation also should be obtained because many of these patients are
nutritionally malnourished. Patients with morbid obesity may benefit from bariatric surgery
before TKA because it has been associated with decreased rates of postoperative
complications25 (Video 4). 
Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is among the more common comorbidities facing patients undergoing
arthroplasty. Diabetes mellitus is associated with perioperative medical complications, such
as pneumonia and stroke.26
Glycemic control, as indicated by a hemoglobin A1c measurement, is predictive of
perioperative complications. A hemoglobin A1c level greater than 8% is predictive of
increased infection rates.27
Patients with diabetes mellitus should be referred to their primary care physician for
preoperative optimization before any arthroplasty procedure and to have good glycemic
control perioperatively (Video 5).
Hepatitis C
Chronic hepatitis C viral infection affects approximately 0.5% of patients in the United
States who undergo primary total joint arthroplasty.28
Patients with hepatitis C have an increased risk for wound complications, infection, and
other postoperative medical complications.
Surgeons should consider referring patients with chronic hepatitis C viral infection for
curative medical treatment preoperatively because recent studies have associated such
treatment with lower rates of postoperative infection.29
Smoking
Tobacco smoke negatively affects endothelial function. This presents a problem for the
wound-healing environment in patients who undergo TKA.
Patients undergoing TKA who smoke have an increased risk for postoperative
complications and revision surgery.30
Patients who smoke should be referred to their primary care physician for smoking
cessation before TKA.
Smoking status can be assessed via a urine cotinine test.

Treatment Options for Knee Osteoarthritis
Treatment options for osteoarthritis: The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Clinical
Practice Guidelines on knee osteoarthritis indicate the strength of recommendation for each
treatment modality.
Self-guided exercise, physical therapy, and activity modifications
Strength of recommendation: strong
Weight loss
Strength of recommendation: moderate
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications
Strength of recommendation: strong
Off-loader bracing or lateral wedge insole
Strength of recommendation: moderate

None of these have good evidence for efficacy. The American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons Clinical Practice Guidelines on knee osteoarthritis do not recommend hyaluronic
acid injections and are inconclusive with regard to platelet-rich plasma and corticosteroids.
Surgical treatment (arthroplasty versus osteotomy)
Workup for patients with knee pain must include evaluation of the spine and hip; therefore,
the patient history should include asking about known pathology or management of these
anatomic structures.

Treatment Options for Knee Osteoarthritis
Numerous treatment options are available for patients with knee pain, depending on the
diagnosis. A nonsurgical treatment approach is recommended for patients with
osteoarthritis or other noninfectious arthridities, with escalation to more invasive
procedures if nonsurgical treatment options fail. In obtaining a patient’s history,
surgeons must understand a patient’s symptoms, duration of symptoms, and treatment
modalities already attempted. In general, treatment should begin with less invasive
modalities and progress to more invasive modalities, as necessary.
For osteoarthritis, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons has evaluated
available treatment options and published clinical practice guidelines.
